analysis.one_liner: Strips the insurance industry's long-standing exemption from federal antitrust rules.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to subject insurers to federal antitrust law was sent to three House committees, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal antitrust law generally bans price-fixing and other restraints of trade, but a 1945 law, the McCarran-Ferguson Act, carved the 'business of insurance' out of that regime. This bill would apply the Federal Trade Commission Act to the parts of the insurance business not regulated by state law, and let the Justice Department and FTC issue joint antitrust enforcement policies for insurer joint activities. It never received so much as a subcommittee vote in any of its three committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurance customers. The bill would expose insurance practices to federal antitrust enforcement, giving regulators more tools against industry-wide joint activities that can keep premiums or other terms uniform; the CRS summary describes it as a bill 'to further competition in the insurance industry' [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so the Federal Trade Commission Act, outside of unfair-competition matters, applies to the business of insurance where that business is not regulated by state law [S2] [S3].

Authorizes the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission to issue joint statements of their antitrust enforcement policies regarding joint activities in the insurance business, signaling tighter scrutiny of industry-wide cooperation [S2] [S3].
Repeals section 3 of the McCarran-Ferguson Act and strikes the FTC Act provision shielding the industry, removing two statutory barriers to federal antitrust enforcement against insurers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which have operated under a federal antitrust exemption since 1945 and would face FTC and DOJ scrutiny of joint activities and coordination that state law does not reach.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves FTC Act application only where the insurance business is not regulated by state law, so much of the industry would remain under state-only oversight and the federal reach would be partial [S2] [S3].

Because the bill targets insurer joint activities, insurance rate-setting and information-sharing arrangements that supporters call benign and insurers say keep markets stable could face litigation costs, which insurers might pass on to policyholders through higher premiums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, targeted rollback of an industry-specific antitrust exemption rather than a sweeping overhaul, so the consumer upside is real but limited — especially since state-regulated insurance activities stay exempt. The strongest objection, that antitrust suits against insurer rate-setting could raise costs for policyholders, is plausible but untested, and the bill's own structure (FTC enforcement only where state law does not reach) limits both sides of the ledger.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and to a subcommittee the next day, it was never marked up, reported out, or voted on, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio (D-OR) introduced the Insurance Industry Competition Act of 2007 on February 15, 2007, with five original cosponsors drawn from both parties [S3] [S4].
The bill's only substantive action was referral: it went to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, the Energy and Commerce and Financial Services Committees [S5].
The next day, February 16, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where the record ends [S5].
No committee held a markup, reported the bill, or scheduled a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, killing the bill [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies came out ahead: by letting the bill die without any committee action, they kept the McCarran-Ferguson exemption from federal antitrust law intact for another Congress.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply federal antitrust law to the insurance business.

for.name: Original cosponsors: Gene Taylor (D-MS), Bobby Jindal (R-LA), Charlie Melancon (D-LA), Rodney Alexander (R-AR), Walter Jones (R-NC)
for.role: Five House cosponsors, split between the parties
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Financial Services committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: None of the three committees referred the bill to took it up; it never received a markup or a hearing on the record.

against.name: Insurance industry trade groups
against.role: Industry lobby defending the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed repealing the insurance antitrust exemption, which protects industry-wide rate-setting and information sharing from federal antitrust suits.

sides.party_line_note: The six named supporters split evenly, 3 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but because the bill never reached a floor vote, the partisan split on the outcome came instead from Democratic-chaired committees that never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would end the industry's 1945-era exemption from the Federal Trade Commission Act where state law does not already regulate the business, exposing joint insurer activities to federal antitrust enforcement. Insurers' interest is in keeping the exemption, which lets them coordinate on rates and terms without federal antitrust risk; that coordination is what the bill's consumers stand to gain from dismantling [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission antitrust enforcers
industries.note: The bill grants DOJ and FTC new authority over insurance and directs them to issue joint enforcement policy statements for insurer joint activities, expanding their jurisdiction over a currently sheltered sector [S2] [S3].
